verdict.summary: TTM Technologies has shifted from a conventional PCB cycle story toward a mix of AI data-center interconnect and defense electronics, but the balance sheet is moving in the opposite direction. Q2 2026 sales crossed $1.0 billion, up 37% year over year; GAAP diluted EPS was $0.77, adjusted EBITDA margin 16.6%, book-to-bill 1.49 and aerospace/defense backlog exceeded $1.7 billion. Management guided Q3 revenue to $1.10-$1.14 billion and raised FY2026 revenue to about $4.4 billion with non-GAAP EPS approaching $5.00. AI demand transmits through higher-layer, higher-speed PCBs and substrates used in switches, accelerators and networking, while defense supplies a separate, backlog-supported engine. The problem is leverage: the Epiq acquisition is all-cash and the current snapshot already shows $1.10 billion debt against $508 million cash. At 27.7x EV/EBITDA the multiple requires successful integration and sustained mix gains. Wait: the $123.36 geometry is archival, not armed. TTMI first needs a fresh RTH structure with dated volume evidence; until then sizing and order fields remain inactive.

business.overview:
TTM manufactures advanced printed circuit boards, RF components and mission-system assemblies. Revenue depends on volume, layer count, technology content and utilization across data-center networking, aerospace/defense, automotive, medical and industrial programs.

AI reaches TTM through the physical interconnect: accelerators, high-radix switches and power-dense racks require high-speed, high-layer-count boards with tighter signal-integrity tolerances. Data-center/networking mix therefore raises content per system, while aerospace/defense adds long-cycle programs and a $1.7B-plus backlog.

The model breaks if hyperscale builds pause, customers redesign boards, yields or utilization disappoint, or defense programs slip. The Epiq acquisition adds capabilities but also all-cash funding, execution and leverage risk just as the equity multiple assumes continued margin expansion. A 1.49 book-to-bill and backlog above $1.7B support visibility, yet aerospace and defense mix carries program, qualification and working-capital timing risk. The critical test is converting data-center demand into margin without allowing acquisition integration or copper and laminate costs to absorb the revenue gain.
business.moat: TTM's moat is qualified manufacturing complexity: high-layer-count PCB process control, RF/microwave integration, trusted defense credentials and the ability to produce at scale across regulated customer programs. It is a manufacturing moat with switching and qualification friction, not proprietary silicon economics, so pricing and utilization still matter.

filings.finding: The Q2 Form 10-Q reports $382.8M Aerospace & Defense segment sales with $63.9M operating income and $621.6M Commercial sales with $112.7M operating income. It also reconciles 104.291M basic to 107.583M diluted weighted-average shares, with 0.084M anti-dilutive awards excluded.

The August 17 Form 8-K records a $1.1B cash purchase of Epiq Solutions, committed $300M term-loan A and $800M seven-year term-loan B funding, and a $77M regulatory termination fee; this is acquisition debt, not equity issuance.

The FY2025 Form 10-K supplies the audited PCB and RF operating baseline, customer and end-market concentration, debt covenants and manufacturing risks used to judge the later Epiq acquisition and incremental secured borrowing.
